analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and restores health law as it stood before 2010.
analysis.headline: A single senator's bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act drew no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and the companion 2010 reconciliation law from the books entirely, restoring the law as if they had never passed. That means ending the premium subsidies that help people buy insurance, the Medicaid expansion, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, the requirement that children can stay on a parent's plan until age 26, and Medicare drug savings. It would also wipe out the taxes created by those laws, which fall mainly on high earners and medical devices. The bill never advanced past its first day: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and nothing more happened for the rest of the two-year Congress [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the clearest financial winners would be high-income households, because the law's 3.8% tax on investment income and its extra Medicare payroll tax on wages above a high threshold would disappear with the rest of the statute. Medical device makers would likewise gain from repeal of the excise tax on their products. Insurers would be freed from coverage rules, though they would also lose the subsidized customer base the law created [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and medical device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the ACA and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 and restores all law they amended as if the statutes had never been enacted [S2][S3].

Because the repeal covers the whole statute, it eliminates the taxes those laws created, including the surtax on net investment income and the additional Medicare tax that apply to higher-income households [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on the millions of people who gained coverage or protections under the law: subsidy recipients, adults covered by the Medicaid expansion, people with pre-existing conditions who would again face denials or surcharges, young adults who would lose access to a parent's plan, and seniors whose Medicare drug out-of-pocket savings would be repealed [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurance subscribers and people with pre-existing conditions

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA would end premium tax credits and the Medicaid expansion, leaving people who get coverage through those programs without the help that pays for it [S2][S3].

The bill contains no replacement for any ACA protection, so guaranteed issue for pre-existing conditions, the ban on annual and lifetime limits, and dependent coverage to age 26 would all vanish, restoring the pre-2010 insurance market [S2][S3].

The bill would also repeal the revenue stream that financed the coverage expansions, so its benefits flow disproportionately to higher-income households while the lost protections and subsidies fall on lower- and middle-income people [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains go mostly to higher earners and device manufacturers, while its costs fall on people who depend on the ACA for coverage, affordability help, or protections. There is no replacement provision in the bill for anything it repeals, so an honest supporter has to concede that millions would lose coverage or financial help on day one [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on January 7, 2015, the first week of the new Congress [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No cosponsors signed on from either party [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber during the 114th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill went nowhere, the Affordable Care Act stayed in place, so people who rely on its subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and pre-existing condition protections kept them. No interest group's position changed as a result of this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting the bill die without action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan bloc ever took a recorded position [S4].

industries.note: Repeal would erase the 3.8% net investment income tax and the additional Medicare payroll tax that apply to wages and investment income above high thresholds, a direct tax cut for the wealthiest households [S3]. The bill offers nothing in return for the coverage losses borne by lower- and middle-income people.

The ACA imposed a 2.3% excise tax on medical device sales, and full repeal would eliminate it. Device makers would keep that windfall while the public loses the coverage programs the tax helped fund [S3].

Repeal would free insurers from coverage rules, medical loss ratio requirements, and the health insurance tax, but it would also strip away the premium subsidies and mandate that brought them millions of subsidized customers. Their gains and losses pull in opposite directions [S2][S3].
